newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's 1st offshore oil rig worries fishermen.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's 1st offshore oil rig worries fishermen.

text.p: As the final touches are being put to state-owned oil exploration company Soekor's new oil rig, fisherman await the start of drilling of South Africa's first oil well with trepidation.

The customised semi-submersible rig, the Orca, is due to start drilling in the Oribi oilfield off Mossel Bay in February and fisherman are concerned this operation will fall in the middle of the South East coast's finest hake fishing grounds, known as "The Blues."
The Orca has been undergoing refurbishment in Simon's Town and is expected to leave for Mossel Bay later this month.
According to the latest issue of SA Commercial Marine, about five square kms of Oribi will initially be a no-go zone to fishermen but this could be increased if more wells are opened up.
The magazine said the fishing industry was equally concerned about the 150-or-so abandoned drill heads in the area that had not been removed and remained in trawling lanes.
The industry wanted Soekor to clean up as its drilling progressed but feared that it would not be feasible economically and technically to remove the old drill heads.
"If this turns out to be correct, then the inexorable growth of the oilfield will have the potential to destroy The Blues," the magazine said.
It said some form of compensation should be paid to fisherman, possibly through shares of the oil revenue as the impact of the operations could exclude the entire area to fishing.
Commenting on the article, Soekor chief executive Joggie Heuser said that every effort had been taken to minimise the effect oil drilling would have on fishing.

The fishing industry had been kept fully informed of the position of the 144 wellheads sunk over the entire South African offshore area. There were originally only seven wellheads in The Blues area, two of which had been removed.

An environmental management programme had been drawn up to minimise the effect of drilling and an independent study by a British research laboratory had confirmed that the exclusion zone affected less that 0.2 percent of The Blues area.
The laboratory had calculated the maximum loss that could be suffered by the fishing industry because of the Oribi would be a maximum of 95,000 rand over six years.

A joint venture between Soekor E&P and Energy Africa Ltd, the Oribi will be South Africa's first offshore oilfield and is expected to initially produce 20,000 barrels of oil a day, with this amount tapering off over three to six years.
It will form the nucleus for the subsequent development of several other nearby oil discoveries, which would extend production life by a further six years.
Soekor and Energy Africa, its 20 percent partner, plan to pump the oil into a one million barrel shuttle tanker for shipment to one of South Africa's three coastal refineries in Cape Town or Durban.
